practice_span: I have painted on walls since I was ten. It has been twenty-six years.
local_belonging_phrase: “Our painting belongs on our wall. Forest, field, dance, all of it is from here.”
ecological_input: We coat the wall with cow dung and red earth. The rice is from our own field, ground to make the white. We chew a bamboo stick to make a brush.
place_change: Now concrete houses have come, and dung walls are fewer. Talk of the highway and the port has raised fear about our land, and the forest has shrunk too.
emotion_about_place_change: “If the wall goes, the painting will move to paper. But if the land goes, what will we paint?”
teacher_name_relation: My grandmother, Sakhubai. She drew the wedding chowk in the village as a suvasini.
teaching_memory: My grandmother sat me in front of the wall. I drew a person, and she said, “What is their work?” I drew again and put a plough in the hand. Then she laughed.
remembered_phrase_gesture: “First the circle, then the work.” Saying this, she would turn the stick in a circle in the air.
family_generations: My grandmother and mother painted. My sister and I paint. My daughter Priya is in school and paints in the holidays. My brother now paints on paper too.
transmission_strength: Children quickly learn the Tarpa dance and field scenes, because they see them every day.
transmission_weakness: The rules of the wedding chowk and the songs that go with it. Few suvasinis who know them are left.
teaching_difficulty: Children's schooling and going to the city for work. Also, they want to learn only what sells fast.
primary_material: Rice flour, cow dung, red earth, a bamboo stick. Canvas or paper for selling.
material_origin: Rice, earth and dung from the village. Bamboo from the forest. Paper and paint from the Dahanu market.
first_contact: Before festivals I coated the walls with my mother. I still remember the coolness of the dung on my hands.
material_special: The rice white becomes one with the wall. It does not shine, but it stands out in the dim light of our homes.
material_in_hands: Mixed with water, the flour should run evenly down the stick. When it is right, the line walks by itself.
material_feels_wrong: If the paint is too thin it runs. If too thick it sticks to the stick and the line breaks.
correction_action: I add a little water or flour and first draw a line on my fingernail to test. Only then do I touch the wall.
material_change_gain: Paper and acrylic took the painting outside. It can be sold, and it doesn't spoil in the rain.
material_change_loss: The shine of acrylic feels false. Without the wall, the link with the festival and the home breaks.
occasion_of_use: The dev chowk at weddings, and on house walls at festivals and harvest.
sensory_scene: The smell of wet dung, the Tarpa playing all night, and in the firelight it seems the white people on the wall are dancing.
remembered_community_phrase: “No chowk, no wedding.” The old women of the village still say this today.
special_vs_everyday: Everyday painting means farming and dance, and it can be sold. The wedding chowk is only for that house.
special_object_rule: Only a suvasini draws the chowk, and songs are sung as it is drawn. The image of Palghat Devi stays there.
not_for_sale_example: The wedding dev chowk and Palghat Devi.
why_protected: She is a goddess, not decoration. We do not accept putting her on a canvas and hanging her on a wall.
safer_alternative: Paintings of the Tarpa dance, farming, forest and festivals. Photos and stories of these can be given.
pride_moment: At an exhibition in Mumbai, a girl stood in the Tarpa circle in front of my painting and began to dance.
recognition_by_others: The knowledgeable women of the village called me to draw the wedding chowk. That is greater than any outside prize.
loss_if_stopped: Our language for telling our stories, our god, and our bond with the land would be gone.
key_stakeholder_of_loss: Our next generation, who would have to read about their own identity in someone else's book.
change_in_lifetime: Earlier nobody thought of selling a painting. Now children earn from it, but there is competition from printed ‘Warli’ mugs.
artisan_initiated_change: I started a Saturday class for village girls, and began attaching a story card to each painting.
desired_keep: The rice white, the circular layout, and the rules of the chowk.
desired_let_go: Prices set by the middleman, and painting in large numbers at low prices.
strength_anchor: I can tell the story of every painting, and my line moves without stopping. I can teach the girls.
concern_anchor: Our painting is printed on mugs, T-shirts and walls, with no name given and not a rupee paid.
shareable_content: Tarpa, farming and forest paintings, my name, and details of my class.
private_content: The wedding chowk, Palghat Devi, the chowk songs and details of the land dispute.
desired_change: Companies using Warli should name the artist, and the village should be paid for it.
desired_continuity: The chowk will not be sold. It will stay in the village, in the hands of the suvasinis.
learning_story: I painted a hundred identical pictures for a shopkeeper. After the fiftieth, the people had no work left, only lines. I remembered my grandmother's question. Since then I paint only a set number a day.
emotional_story: After my grandmother died, her house wall collapsed in the rain, with the chowk on it. The next year we coated a new wall using that same earth.
clarification_story: A woman said, what is there to this, just triangles. I gave her the stick and asked her to draw the Tarpa circle. She saw at once that one wrong line breaks the circle.
outsider_misunderstanding: People think Warli is an easy design. It is our prayer and our history.
